newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac closely follows U.S. probe into TWA crash.
newsitem.headline: Chirac closely follows U.S. probe into TWA crash.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac said on Thursday he was closely following the U.S. investigation into the TWA flight 800 disaster while a lawyer for the some of the French victims' families criticised the inquiry for taking so long in reaching a decision.
"I have personally followed the developments of the investigation led with determination by the American authorities," Chirac said in a statement.

"I will continue to contribute, in close cooperation with our American friends, the greatest attention to the investigation so that everything may be known about the tragedy that has struck you," he wrote.

Chirac's message was addressed to relatives of the 47 French nationals who were among 230 people killed a year ago when the Paris-bound jumbo exploded over the Atlantic minutes after takeoff from New York.

Hundreds of relatives and friends have gathered in New York to commemorate the disaster. French relatives have repeatedly expressed frustration with the pace of a U.S. probe, which has yet to determine the exact cause of an explosion aboard.
A lawyer for French families of some of the victims, Gilles-Jean Portejoie, suggested that the U.S. investigators might be stalling.
"It seems surprising that the cause is not known after a year and when almost everything has been recovered," he told France Info radio.

"I don't want this conclusion to be a non-conclusion. My feeling is that today international public opinion is being prepared for that," he said. "The families...will not accept that. They will not accept that the truth not be uncovered."
"France, on this July 17, shares your grief. It is at your sides," Chirac said in his message.
"It's an absolute necessity, firstly to respect your lost parents or children, but also to contribute to improve air safety which concerns us all," he added.
Investigators say an explosion in the plane's near-empty centre fuel tank caused it to disintegrate off Long Island on July 17 last year, but they have not determined why.
FBI officials say there is no evidence of a criminal act such as a bomb or a missile destroyed the plane, but they are not ready to declare that a mechanical fault caused the crash.

Families fear that an open conclusion, even if the evidence pointed to mechanical failure, could undermine compensation claims against TWA and absolve air companies of having to make costly safety upgrades.
